title: Genesis 44:1–17
context: After the feast, Joseph orders sacks filled and money returned—and his silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s grain. The brothers are overtaken, searched from eldest to youngest, and the cup is found. They tear their clothes, fall before Joseph, and Judah confesses a guilt God has found out. Joseph will keep only the man with the cup and send the rest home in peace—the test of whether they will abandon Rachel’s other son as they once sold Joseph.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: How earlier teachers on both sides handled the silver cup and the youngest found guilty, quoted directly.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants—Referring to the injury they had formerly done to Joseph, for which they thought God was now reckoning with them. Even in those afflictions wherein we apprehend ourselves wronged by men, yet we must own that God is righteous, and finds out our iniquity. Age and experience may make men wiser and better. They that had sold Joseph, yet would not abandon Benjamin.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 44:16)

reformed.quote: Here Moses relates how skillfully Joseph had contrived to try the dispositions of his brethren. We have said elsewhere that, whereas God has various methods of chastising men, he yet especially tries them by this test, whether they have the fear of God before their eyes. Joseph, therefore, that he may know whether his brethren are changed, brings them into new danger.

verses.text: He commanded the steward of his house, saying, “Fill the men’s sacks with food, as much as they can carry, and put each man’s money in his sack’s mouth.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joseph commands filling and the old trick of money in the mouth of each sack. Generosity is true; the test is not finished.

Providence can use a brother’s ruse without making the brothers puppets. They will still have to choose what they do when Benjamin is framed.
verses.reformedNotes:
The steward obeys a hidden plan. Food and money go first; the cup is next.

God who sent Joseph ahead (45:5–8) can govern even this setup. The brothers will meet their past in a sack they did not pack.

verses.text: Put my cup, the silver cup, in the sack’s mouth of the youngest, with his grain money.” He did according to the word that Joseph had spoken.
verses.arminianNotes:
The silver cup goes in the youngest’s sack, with his grain-money. Benjamin is made to look like the thief.

Classical Arminians: the trap is severe, yet the moral crisis it creates is no pretense. Will they sacrifice the beloved son again?
verses.reformedNotes:
Youngest and cup are paired on purpose. Joseph aims the test at the brother who stands where he once stood in Jacob’s heart.

A particular sack, a particular son. Providence is not vague.

verses.text: As soon as the morning was light, the men were sent away, they and their donkeys.
verses.arminianNotes:
Morning light, they are sent away with the donkeys. The road looks like mercy—full sacks, no delay.

Apparent ease can be the front of a trial. Grace does not always announce the test at the gate.
verses.reformedNotes:
Dawn dispatch is Joseph’s timing. They leave as free men so the overtaking will sting more.

The LORD who times famines also times this short head start.

verses.text: When they had gone out of the city, and were not yet far off, Joseph said to his steward, “Up, follow after the men. When you overtake them, ask them, ‘Why have you rewarded evil for good?
verses.arminianNotes:
A short distance, then: Up, follow—Why have you rewarded evil for good? The charge is spoken before they know the cup is theirs to explain.

They are accused of a theft they did not plan. Still, the old evil they did plan is not far from the words.
verses.reformedNotes:
Overtaking is ordered, not accidental. “Evil for good” is Joseph’s line; God can mean more by it than Joseph does.

Repaid evil is the family history, now staged on the road.

verses.text: Isn’t this that from which my lord drinks, and by which he indeed divines? You have done evil in so doing.’”
verses.arminianNotes:
Drink and divination: the cup is dressed as a lord’s sacred tool. The charge is made to feel religious, not petty.

Joseph’s Egyptian mask includes a claim he may not even practice. The brothers must answer the scene they are in, not the brother they cannot yet see.
verses.reformedNotes:
Divination-speech fits the viceroy they think they face. The cup is bait and symbol.

God needs no cup to know; the brothers are being measured by a wiser eye than Egypt’s.

verses.text: He overtook them, and he spoke these words to them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The steward says exactly those words. The script arrives intact.

Classical Arminians: a faithful messenger can still deliver a hard sentence. The brothers now have to reply.
verses.reformedNotes:
Overtaken, they hear Joseph’s voice in a servant’s mouth.

Means stay ordinary—a steward, a road, a sentence—while the Author of the larger story is not finished.

verses.text: They said to him, “Why does my lord speak such words as these? Far be it from your servants that they should do such a thing!
verses.arminianNotes:
Far be it from your servants. Their protest is sincere about this theft.

Pastorally: they can be innocent of the cup and still not innocent of Joseph. Honesty here is not in doubt; it is not yet full repentance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Shock is not the same as righteousness. They truly did not steal this cup.

Providence can convict through a charge that is, at street level, false.

verses.text: Behold, the money, which we found in our sacks’ mouths, we brought again to you out of the land of Canaan. How then should we steal silver or gold out of your lord’s house?
verses.arminianNotes:
They cite the money they already brought back from Canaan. Why then steal silver or gold?

Prior honesty is offered as evidence. Grace can use a true defense even when a deeper guilt is still unnamed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Returned money is their exhibit A. The argument is sound as far as it goes.

God let them return the silver in chapter 43 so this protest would have weight—and still fail to open Benjamin’s sack clean.

verses.text: With whomever of your servants it is found, let him die, and we also will be my lord’s slaves.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They swear death for the one found with it, and slavery for the rest. Rash zeal overplays the hand.

Arminians warn: confident oaths can become the noose. They bind themselves beyond what wisdom required.
verses.reformedNotes:
A death-and-slavery vow they will not be asked to keep in full. The steward will soften it; the test will not.

Words said in panic still sit in the record of this family.

verses.text: He said, “Now also let it be according to your words. He with whom it is found will be my slave; and you will be blameless.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The steward scales it down: the one with the cup will be servant; the rest innocent. An escape hatch is held out.

They could take the out and go home without Benjamin—the old pattern. The next verses will show whether they will.
verses.reformedNotes:
Innocent rest, enslaved youngest: that is the offer Joseph wanted on the table.

The door to abandon Rachel’s son is opened on purpose. What they do with it will tell the truth.

verses.text: Then they hurried, and each man took his sack down to the ground, and each man opened his sack.
verses.arminianNotes:
Sacks down, sacks open, quickly. They expect to be cleared.

Speed can be integrity. They are not stalling; they still do not know Benjamin’s mouth holds the cup.
verses.reformedNotes:
Quick emptying is confidence. God lets them open every sack in public.

Exposure will be orderly, eldest to youngest, so no one can say the search was random.

verses.text: He searched, beginning with the oldest, and ending at the youngest. The cup was found in Benjamin’s sack.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eldest to youngest—then the cup in Benjamin’s sack. The last brother is the one framed.

The beloved is made to look guilty. The test now lands on whether love will stay with him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Search order retraces birth order until Rachel’s son. Joseph watches the old wound reopen.

The cup is where Joseph placed it, and where God meant the heart to be searched.

verses.text: Then they tore their clothes, and each man loaded his donkey, and returned to the city.
verses.arminianNotes:
Clothes torn, donkeys loaded, they return to the city. No one takes the steward’s offer to leave Benjamin.

Arminians mark the turn: they go back together. Grace has been training this loyalty since the money in the sacks first frightened them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Tearing clothes is covenant grief, not theater only. Every man loads up—shared return.

The same men who once walked away from a pit now walk back toward a throne.

verses.text: Judah and his brothers came to Joseph’s house, and he was still there. They fell on the ground before him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Judah is named first as they fall before Joseph, who is still there. The dream of sheaves is on the floor again.

Falling down is not yet the speech of 18–34, but it is already a different Judah than Genesis 37.
verses.reformedNotes:
Judah and his brothers: the leader of the sale now leads the return.

They fall while Joseph is still in the house. Providence kept him from leaving so this bow would happen.

verses.text: Joseph said to them, “What deed is this that you have done? Don’t you know that such a man as I can indeed do divination?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joseph keeps the mask: what deed is this? A man as I can practice divination. He will not thaw yet.

The pressure stays on so the confession will be theirs, not extracted by a hug too soon.
verses.reformedNotes:
Joseph again claims to practice divination. He speaks as Egypt’s lord, not as brother.

God often lets the trial run to the sentence before the name is revealed.

verses.text: Judah said, “What will we tell my lord? What will we speak? How will we clear ourselves? God has found out the iniquity of your servants. Behold, we are my lord’s slaves, both we and he also in whose hand the cup is found.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Judah: what shall we say? God has found out the iniquity of your servants. He will not parse cup-theft from the older crime.

Conscience names God as the finder. The cup is the occasion; the guilt is larger, and they own it together rather than dumping it on Benjamin.
verses.reformedNotes:
“God has found out” is the theological heart of the scene. Hidden sin is not hidden from the LORD.

Judah speaks for all. Providence has used a planted cup to surface a sold brother.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear guilt before God, not mere bad luck. Arminians stress a free, now-willing confession under convicting grace; Reformed readers stress that God found them out by a counsel they did not script.

verses.text: He said, “Far be it from me that I should do so. The man in whose hand the cup is found, he will be my slave; but as for you, go up in peace to your father.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joseph refuses mass slavery: only the man with the cup; you go up in peace to your father. The knife is peace without Benjamin.

Arminian climax of the test: they may leave. Grace has brought them to a live choice—repeat Genesis 37, or stay.
verses.reformedNotes:
Far be it from me—Joseph plays just judge and offers a clean road home.

“Peace to your father” is the one sentence that cannot be peace if Benjamin stays. The next speech will answer.
